subject: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs

messages.author: ee725f7de3d79c3f
messages.subject: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Hi group! 

I  was curious, if anyone has any ideas regarding how you to incorporate information on marking success into a spatially-explicit capture-recapture model. I’m not sure there’s a way to do that using the SECR package, but maybe someone has a good lead to investigate?

We are working on setting hair snare corrals for black bear, and we are unsure if the hair snares are effective at marking cubs. After a pilot season this last summer, we decided on using clusters of hair snare corrals spread across our study area. We are planning to set 4 hair snare corrals per cluster, 3 with a single-strand of barbed wire at 45 cm and 1 using 2-strands of wire at 20 cm and 50 cm. We’ll use teeth from bears harvested in 2020 to see if the proportion of yearlings (cubs during the 2019 hair snaring spree) marked by hair snares matched the proportion in which we set single- and double-stranded sites (i.e., if cubs were equally marked, we would expect that 75% of the marked cubs would show up on the single-stranded sites and 25% at the double-stranded sites).  We’re doing this more for an assurance since past literature suggests that cubs should be marked, but if we do find that cubs are missing the wire in single-stranded sites, how could we revise our population estimate? It's more of a hypothetical-case as we don't have the data yet, but are there ways to revise a population estimate by incorporating that source of data? Or maybe we can't?

Thanks for any feedback!

Laura

messages.author: 3908a2da5354fc44
messages.subject: RE: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Laura,

 

Just a few comments that may not directly address your question.  First, the probability of capturing a cub is not going to be independent of capturing the sow, which is problematic for most capture-recapture models. I think your point estimate will be ok (Murray can correct me if I’m wrong), but the variance will likely be underestimated.

 

Second, the home range size of females with cubs is going to be much different from a solitary female or a female with yearlings depending on the time of year (the younger the cubs the smaller the home range of mother with cubs). These differences in home range size could lead to heterogeneity in the sigma parameter (maybe secr is robust to this violation – not sure). I think the later in summer you can do the hair snaring the better.

 

Third, your trap spatial design leads me to question whether it could affect your estimate of sigma. If you place these corrals in clusters are you treating each corral as a single trap, or the cluster as a single trap? If the former, could that lead to underestimating sigma? If a bear is likely to visit multiple corrals in a cluster much more than multiple clusters your estimate of sigma could be underestimated.

 

Finally, have you considered trying to collect independent auxiliary data? If you can estimate the number of females via secr (N-hat-females) and have an independent estimate of the number of cubs per female (c-hat-per-female), you could estimate the number of cubs as N-hat-females x c-hat-per-female. You could use the delta method to get a measure of precision on this estimate assuming you obtain a SE for your per capita cubs estimate.

 

Regards,

 

Duane

messages.author: 78ef92d8ca24b10c
messages.subject: Re: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Hey Laura,
  • To me, a good sampling design intends to limit nuisance variability as much as possible. If there is some size/age related variability in detection, the design you're describing seems like it could be inducing an interaction between something that is relatively well known (the characteristics of the traps) and something that is unknown (the size or age of the bears leaving hair, unless you're also trying to do some sort of aging with telomeres or something). Without an individual covariate for size/age, I think you might be stuck with using a finite mixture or an individual random effect (and if certain parts of the population cannot ever be captured, you can't model this at all). I dunno, maybe simplifying the design is the easiest way to approach this.
  • You could try to get some more information about any sampling bias, maybe using cameras (images or video) to see you can observe anything that would suggest some sort of bias in hair deposition|visitation. Visitation and deposition could be decomposed in a modeling exercise (Ben Augustine just built some options to perform analyses like this into his package), but maybe at the least visual evidence gives you a better sense of how to define the population being sampled (all bears, adult bears, whatever). 
  • Duane raises good points about non-independence in the detection of individual animals if there are cubs and sows moving around together (the little I've seen positive/negative dependence explored in simulation suggests relatively small negative bias either way, but?). One other thing to consider is that sampling siblings that are moving around together may put a little more pressure on the lab to do a good job at discriminating individual genotypes.
John

messages.author: 0dbfcf0efe4ff8fe
messages.subject: Re: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Good day Laura,

We try to set the wire strand at a consistent 50 cm from the ground, and assume that this excludes cubs and yearlings from the sample. Data from many handled bears indicates that yearlings are not this tall at the shoulder when we sample.  This avoids correlated detections of family groups, so we treat observations as independent.  We consider our SECR-model derived density estimates specific to bears aged 2 years and older.  These are useful for management, and for investigating differences in space and time.  When desired, we estimate total densities by using information about population age structure to add dependent offspring to estimates for bears aged 2 + years.

However, we don't have concurrent, study-area specific age structure information, so this is a source of error and uncertainty in estimates of total bear density. Also, because it's hard to keep the wire at a consistent height, and bear movement/posture isn't predictable, we probably do sample some yearlings, though at a lower rate.  We may also miss some 2-year olds that visit traps. We often see support for individual heterogeneity in g0 (within sexes), and I wonder if this is (partly) attributable to rare captures of yearlings and reduced detectability of 2-year olds.  If we fit heterogeneity models to data that include rare captures of yearlings, our (inflated) estimates are not really specific to bears aged 2+ years, and we overestimate total density if we add the expected density/number of 0 and 1 year olds to our estimates.  I'll be interested to see the results of your study with both trap types, as our methods for dealing with reduced detectabiltiy of young bears are imperfect at best.  To address this, we are camera-trapping (with video) at some of our corrals, looking for evidence that our data include samples from yearlings and cubs. Failing to record such capture events still wouldn't mean they never happen. 

In your situation, I can't think how to directly model the effect of trap type (1 or 2 strand) on g0 of cubs, because you won't have age information to that would allow you fit an e.g. age class X trap type interaction term.  You will detect smaller, younger bears (many at 2-strand traps and a few at 1-strand traps), so it might make sense to evaluate models that include individual heterogeneity (e.g. using a 2-point fininte mixture on g0, within sexes), and if they're supported, estimate total bear density (including cubs and yearlings) from those models. ... oh, sorry, this is exactly what John said...

You could try to minimize individual heterogeneity in sigma (e.g. between females with and without cubs) via the timing of sampling, or try to model it using a mixture distribution on sigma (within sexes).

You will violate the independence assumption somewhat. Options for avoiding this assumption or adjusting for overdispersion when estimating variances are not as well developed as in nonspatial CR, but might be worth looking into. 

Regarding your clustered design, 

Can you distribute clusters according to some randomized or systematic design such that you get a spatially representative sample of the entire region of interest? See Buckland et al's books (2001, 2015), and documentation for empirical.varD(), trap.builder() and associated references.

There's no need to treat the cluster as one trap, though there are options for treating clusters as spatial replicates when estimating variances. Several studies (Sollmann et al. 2012, Wilton et al. 2014, Sun et al. 2014, Clark 2018 or 2019) have investigated the efficacy of different designs, including within-cluster trap spacings, in this exact context.  So, with some prior information about home range size, you should be able to design a survey to obtain enough spatial recaptures of both sexes to inform sigma.  I think Sun et al. recommended a minimum of 4 traps per cluster... my personal recommendation is to avoid such minima and have more.

Good luck!
Eric

messages.author: ee725f7de3d79c3f
messages.subject: Re: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Thanks for your thoughts, Duane!

 

We're constrained in our sampling efforts to May and June as dog training for free-roaming bear starts July 1st in our state, and as a precaution, we are tearing down all sites by that deadline to avoid any potential issues with dogs running into barbed wire.  I anticipate we will somewhat violate the assumption of independence because of sows with cubs, so I'll look more into how we can adjust variance estimates to reflect that.

 

Each hair corral will be a single trap, and they are close enough together that we anticipate that a bear can visit multiple corrals in a cluster and potentially can move to different clusters. We are using a peanut butter/oil slurry that mainly soaks into the ground and into sticks/leaf litter so the bears don't have a strong food reward. We didn't notice any strong "trap happy" response during our pilot.

 

We haven't considered trying to collect independent auxiliary data, but maybe that is something we should look into further. Thanks!

messages.author: ee725f7de3d79c3f
messages.subject: Re: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Hi John and Eric,  (and sorry to the entire group for double-posting on this thread.. I should have replied to all responses in one message)

Thanks for the replies. We used cameras at some of our pilot sites which is what spurred our thoughts on whether we were actually marking cubs. John, What package are you referring to regarding decomposing visitation and deposition? We've discussed using a finite-mixture to incorporate individual heterogeneity on g0 or sigma, but I can see this all getting pretty complicated and maybe simplifying would be the best approach. I like the idea of using cameras to give us a better sense of how to define the population we are sampling, which sounds like what Eric is doing. We only put cameras out on a handful of sites during our pilot season, but it could be worth another (better) look. 

Eric, as for our study design, we tested multiple designs using secrdesign with prior information about home range size and density to make sure we can obtain enough spatial recaptures to run these models. We have clusters of hair corrals systematically spaced so that we have a spatially representative sample of the entire region of interest. Another thank you for your perspective on how you identify your population of interest and information on what you're seeing from handled bears. 

- Laura

On Saturday, March 30, 2019 at 1:37:49 PM UTC-5, John wrote:
Hey Laura,
  • To me, a good sampling design intends to limit nuisance variability as much as possible. If there is some size/age related variability in detection, the design you're describing seems like it could be inducing an interaction between something that is relatively well known (the characteristics of the traps) and something that is unknown (the size or age of the bears leaving hair, unless you're also trying to do some sort of aging with telomeres or something). Without an individual covariate for size/age, I think you might be stuck with using a finite mixture or an individual random effect (and if certain parts of the population cannot ever be captured, you can't model this at all). I dunno, maybe simplifying the design is the easiest way to approach this.
  • You could try to get some more information about any sampling bias, maybe using cameras (images or video) to see you can observe anything that would suggest some sort of bias in hair deposition|visitation. Visitation and deposition could be decomposed in a modeling exercise (Ben Augustine just built some options to perform analyses like this into his package), but maybe at the least visual evidence gives you a better sense of how to define the population being sampled (all bears, adult bears, whatever). 
  • Duane raises good points about non-independence in the detection of individual animals if there are cubs and sows moving around together (the little I've seen positive/negative dependence explored in simulation suggests relatively small negative bias either way, but?). One other thing to consider is that sampling siblings that are moving around together may put a little more pressure on the lab to do a good job at discriminating individual genotypes.
John

messages.author: 2c49652a5796ed9c
messages.subject: Re: Hair snare corrals for black bears and marking cubs
parts:
Regarding separating visitation from deposition. I tackled this issue within classical capture-recapture with the goal of accounting for the fact that you cannot know the first capture occasion with certainty in model Mb when hair samples are subsampled and/or individual identity is lost due to failed DNA amplification.

https://besjournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/2041-210X.12289

Luckily for everyone, SCR seems extremely robust to this problem, at least in the sampling scenarios I've looking into. In this paper, I pointed out that in order to account for individuals that visit a trap and leave no hair sample, you'd need to co-deploy cameras. I believe I said it is unlikely anyone would do that because of costs, but here we are 5 years later and people are indeed doing it.

I believe the model John was referring to is one I posted on the spatial listserv a while ago. It is John's multimethod model (essentially) where individual identity is not known for the camera detections.

https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/eap.1587

This model will allow you to use the camera data to inform density and other parameters by probabilistically resolving the individual identities of camera detections using their spatial location. It accounts for the dependence between the SCR and occupancy detection processes. I don't think this model will help answer your question, however. The main use of this type of model would be to improve the precision of demographic parameter estimates, but the extent to which it would varies by most parameter values. It's possible you could use age class classified photos at the co-deployed sites to estimate age class-specific density, but I expect you would need better data than is possible to collect to do this successfully.

Happy to talk more if you're interested.

Ben
